segments.say: Lesson 6. Sorting & Searching Basics. Linear search, how bubble sort and merge sort work (animated), why O of n log n matters, and using Python's sort with keys.

Sorting puts items in order (smallest to largest, A to Z). Searching finds an item. Once data is sorted, many problems get dramatically faster. Here is an analogy. Finding a name in a jumbled pile of exam papers means checking every paper. If the papers are sorted alphabetically, you can open the pile near the right letter immediately.

Why does this matter? "Sort first" is the opening move for two pointers, intervals, greedy problems and detecting duplicates. Interviewers ask how sorting works and what it costs. In practice you'll call Python's sort(), but you must know it's O of n log n. A few key words. Linear search: Check items one by one: O of n. Comparison sort: Sorts by comparing pairs; the best possible is O of n log n. Stable sort: Equal items keep their original order. In-place: Sorts inside the same list without a copy. Divide & conquer: Split the problem, solve the halves, combine (merge sort).

segments.sec: Watch: Bubble sort: the simplest sort
segments.say: Bubble sort: the simplest sort. Idea: walk through the list comparing neighbours, and swap any pair that's in the wrong order.

segments.sec: Watch: Bubble sort: the simplest sort
segments.say: Compare a index 0=5 and a index 1=1. 5 greater than 1, so they're out of order.

segments.sec: Watch: Bubble sort: the simplest sort
segments.say: . swap leads to 1, 5, 4, 2.

segments.sec: Watch: Bubble sort: the simplest sort
segments.say: 5 greater than 4 leads to swap leads to 1, 4, 5, 2.

segments.sec: Watch: Bubble sort: the simplest sort
segments.say: 5 greater than 2 leads to swap leads to 1, 4, 2, 5. After one full pass, the largest value has "bubbled" to the end, where it stays.

segments.sec: Watch: Bubble sort: the simplest sort
segments.say: Pass 2: 1 less than 4 no swap; 4 greater than 2 swap leads to 1, 2, 4, 5. Now 4 is in place too.

segments.sec: Watch: Bubble sort: the simplest sort
segments.say: Sorted! But two nested loops means ~n squared comparisons: O of n squared. Too slow for big inputs, which is why merge sort exists.

segments.sec: Watch: Merge sort: split, then merge
segments.say: Merge sort: split, then merge. Divide and conquer: split the list in half again and again until each piece has 1 element (a single element is already sorted).

segments.sec: Watch: Merge sort: split, then merge
segments.say: Halve, halve again. log₂(8) equals 3 levels of splitting.

segments.sec: Watch: Merge sort: split, then merge
segments.say: Now merge back up. Merging two sorted lists is easy: repeatedly take the smaller front element.

segments.sec: Watch: Merge sort: split, then merge
segments.say: 27,38 plus 3,43 leads to compare fronts 27 versus 3, take 3; then 27 versus 43, take 27; and so on.

segments.sec: Watch: Merge sort: split, then merge
segments.say: Each level does n work and there are log n levels: O of n log n. Python's built-in sort (Timsort) is also O of n log n.
Sorting in Python (what you will actually use). Here is the code. Pause the video to read it line by line.

When to sort first. You need pairs or triplets that sum to a target leads to sort plus two pointers. Duplicates become neighbours after sorting. Interval and scheduling problems leads to sort by start or end. Greedy choices ("take the smallest first"). Cost: O of n log n added, which is usually fine for n less than or equal to 10 to the 5 or so.
Say it in the interview. "I'll sort first, which costs O of n log n. After that, equal values are adjacent and I can use two pointers in O of n, so O of n log n overall.".

Sorting algorithms. Bubble / insertion / selection: O of n squared, O of 1, teaching only; insertion is OK for tiny or nearly-sorted data. Merge sort: O of n log n, O of n, stable, predictable. Quick sort: O of n log n avg, O of n squared worst, O of log n, fast in practice. Heap sort: O of n log n, O of 1, not stable. Timsort (Python): O of n log n, O of n, stable, great on real data. Counting / bucket: O of n plus k, O of k, small integer ranges only.
Problem 1: Contains Duplicate. Return True if any value appears at least twice in the array. For example, with nums equals 1, 2, 3, 1, the answer is True. 1 appears twice

The obvious brute force: Compare every pair (i, j): two nested loops. That costs O of n squared time. The smart way: Option A: sort, then duplicates sit next to each other, giving O of n log n. Option B (best): a set of values seen so far gives O of 1 "have I seen this?" checks, O of n total. Step by step: seen equals empty set. Then, For each x: if x is in seen, return True; else add it. Then, Return False after the loop.
Here is the Python solution. Complexity: O of n time, O of n space. Pause and read through it, then try writing it yourself without looking.

Problem 2: Merge Sorted Array. nums1 has m sorted numbers followed by n empty slots (0s); nums2 has n sorted numbers. Merge nums2 into nums1 in place so nums1 becomes fully sorted. For example, with nums1 equals 1,2,3,0,0,0, m equals 3, nums2 equals 2,5,6, n equals 3, the answer is nums1 equals 1,2,2,3,5,6.

The obvious brute force: Copy nums2 into the empty slots and call sort(). That costs O((m+n) log(m+n)) time. The smart way: Both lists are already sorted, so merge them like merge sort, but fill from the back: the largest remaining item goes into the last empty slot. Filling from the back never overwrites numbers you still need. Step by step: i equals m minus 1 (end of nums1's real numbers), j equals n minus 1 (end of nums2), k equals m+n minus 1 (last slot). Then, Put the bigger of nums1 index i and nums2 index j at k; move that pointer and k left. Then, Repeat until nums2 is used up.
Here is the Python solution. Complexity: O of m plus n time, O of 1 space. Pause and read through it, then try writing it yourself without looking.

Problem 3: Sort Colors. An array contains only 0s, 1s and 2s (red, white, blue). Sort it in place in one pass without calling sort(). For example, with nums equals 2, 0, 2, 1, 1, 0, the answer is 0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2.

The obvious brute force: Count how many 0s, 1s and 2s there are, then overwrite the array. That's two passes, which is acceptable but not one pass. That costs O of n time, 2 passes. The smart way: Dutch national flag with three pointers: everything before lo is 0, everything after hi is 2, and mid scans. Swap 0s to the front and 2s to the back. Step by step: lo equals mid equals 0, hi equals n minus 1. Then, nums index mid equals 0: swap with lo, then lo++ and mid++. Then, equals 1: mid++. Then, equals 2: swap with hi, hi minus minus (don't move mid, since the swapped-in value is unchecked).
Here is the Python solution. Complexity: O of n time, O of 1 space. Pause and read through it, then try writing it yourself without looking.

A likely interview question: What does sorting cost, and when is it worth it? A strong answer: O of n log n. It's worth it when order unlocks a faster method: two pointers, adjacent duplicates, interval merging, greedy choices, binary search.
